report:
## Conclusion

For most people, regularly taking vitamin C supplements does **not** prevent colds. Large randomized trials analyzed in the authoritative Cochrane systematic review (29 trials, >11,000 general-population participants) found no meaningful reduction in cold incidence from routine daily vitamin C use. There was, however, a modest but consistent benefit in *duration* and *severity* of colds already occurring—about an 8% shorter cold in adults and 14% in children—when vitamin C was taken regularly (not just after symptoms start, since starting vitamin C after a cold begins has no effect).

One notable exception: people under brief but extreme physical or cold stress—such as marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers in subarctic conditions—showed roughly a 50% reduction in cold incidence with regular vitamin C supplementation (pooled RR 0.48, from five trials, 598 participants). This suggests vitamin C may specifically help offset the immune-suppressing effects of intense physical exertion or cold exposure, rather than working as a general cold preventive.

Because these benefits are small for the general population, mainstream medical sources (Mayo Clinic, NCBI/InformedHealth) advise that routine mega-dose vitamin C supplementation for cold prevention is not justified for most healthy adults, though it remains harmless at standard doses and may offer a slight reduction in cold duration.

**Bottom line:** Vitamin C does not meaningfully prevent colds in the general population, though it may modestly shorten cold duration and could roughly halve cold risk for those under intense physical/cold stress.

**Sources:**
- Cochrane review (Hemilä & Chalker, 2013): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/
- NCBI/InformedHealth summary: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/
- PubMed abstract of Cochrane review: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/
- Mayo Clinic News Network: https://newsnetwork.mayoclinic.org/discussion/mayo-clinic-minute-can-vitamin-c-keep-the-common-cold-away/
